facts.raw_span: A 14-year-old girl presented with a 6-year history of a photosensitive eruption involving her face, neck, trunk, and extremities
Her symptoms began at age 8 years

She had previously tried multiple medications including systemic steroids, hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclosporine, tacrolimus, tofacitinib, rituximab, and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), with minimal improvement
Violaceous erythema on forehead and midface
Diffuse poikiloderma involving upper chest, anterolateral thighs, and extensor arms
Erythematous, flat-topped papules on extensor joints of hands
Nailfold examination showed dilated capillary loops, capillary dropout, and ragged cuticles
Elevated serum IFN-β levels (8 pg/mL, normal ≤2 pg/mL)
Presence of anti-TIF-1γ autoantibodies
Radiographic evidence of myositis
Confirmatory skin biopsy performed

concepts.why: The patient's symptoms, including photosensitive eruption, violaceous erythema, and diffuse poikiloderma, along with elevated serum IFN-β levels and presence of anti-TIF-1γ autoantibodies, are consistent with Juvenile Dermatomyositis.

The patient's symptoms, including photosensitive eruption and erythematous papules, along with elevated serum IFN-β levels and presence of autoantibodies, could be consistent with Lupus Erythematosus.
The patient's symptoms, including violaceous erythema, diffuse poikiloderma, and myositis, could be consistent with Mixed Connective Tissue Disease.
The patient's symptoms, including diffuse poikiloderma and nailfold changes, could be consistent with Scleroderma.
The patient's symptoms, including erythematous papules and myositis, could be consistent with Rheumatoid Arthritis.
The patient's elevated serum IFN-β levels and presence of autoantibodies could be consistent with Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia.
The patient's symptoms, including photosensitive eruption and violaceous erythema, could be consistent with Vasculitis.
The patient's symptoms, including diffuse poikiloderma and nailfold changes, could be consistent with Sjögren's Syndrome.
The confirmatory skin biopsy performed explains the diagnosis of Dermatomyositis.
